warp.d: 2D sprite engine on wgpu, its editor, and the SDK a game is written on
warp.x: Warp is a 2D sprite engine built on wgpu, together with an editor built on that engine and an SDK crate that games are written against. A game on Warp is a Rust crate that depends on warp_sdk and implements one trait, Renderer. The engine owns the window, the GPU device and the frame loop, and it calls the game once per frame. The editor opens such a crate as a project and drives its panels from what the game publish

getting-started.d: New project, the starter game, cargo run, the panels, and the smoke test
getting-started.x: Getting started with Warp means making a Rust crate that depends on warp_sdk, implements Renderer, and starts the engine with run. The usual route is to copy the worked starter, which the editor's New Project command also writes. The starter is a small complete game, so a new project begins with a title screen, a pause menu, saves and passing tests. This article covers the project layout, the first run, the editor pa

renderer.d: The entry point, the frame loop, RenderContext, viewports, and DisplaySettings
renderer.x: Renderer and run are the entry point of a Warp game: Renderer is the trait that a game implements, and run is the function that opens the window and calls it once per frame. Both are re-exported at the root of warp_sdk, with Config, RenderContext, DisplaySettings and SharedGpu. A game is one type that implements Renderer. For a game with title and pause screens, shell offers run_shell as an alternative to writing tho

shell.d: Ready title, pause, settings, tutorial and HUD around any game
shell.x: The game shell is a ready player-facing layer that wraps a game in a title screen, a pause menu, a settings screen, a guided tutorial and a HUD at the correct scale. It lives in the warp_sdk::shell module. A game implements ShellGame in place of Renderer, starts with run_shell in place of run, and supplies content and no styling. The shell suits a game that wants those screens with no further design. The front kits a

smoke.d: Boot a game with no window, and play it from a script
smoke.x: The smoke test is the headless proof that a Warp game runs and that a player can play it, with no window and no GPU requirement. It lives in the warp_sdk::smoke module. boot drives the frame loop of a Renderer for a number of frames, and play also sends a Script of keys and mouse events and reports which screens the game went through. A panic fails the run, and a clean return is a game that runs.

front.d: Title and pause menus, save slots, and the settings model and page
front.x: The front end is the family of kits that a game uses for its title screen, pause menu, end screen, save slots and settings. It lives in the warp_sdk::front module, which holds three submodules and nothing else: front::menu, front::save and front::settings. Each submodule has one owner, and a game uses the full path. The family supplies parts that a game composes, and the game keeps its own screen state.

front-menu.d: Title, pause and end screens, painted buttons, five layouts, one focus
front-menu.x: Menu screens are the title, pause and end screens of a game, with the button that they share, in the warp_sdk::front::menu module. A game keeps one Title, Pause or End value, calls show each frame from gui, and gets an optional MenuAction back. The kit paints with the egui painter and uses no stock egui button. It handles focus, the mouse, the keyboard and a gamepad, and the game decides what each action does.

front-save.d: Numbered save files with metadata, atomic writes, and a version check
front-save.x: Save slots are numbered save files with metadata, in the warp_sdk::front::save module. Slots manages a fixed number of files for one game, writes each one atomically, and checks versions on read. The payload is text that the game owns. Fields is a small key=value map for a game that has no format of its own.

front-settings.d: One typed settings model, its file, and a six-tab page to edit it
front-settings.x: Settings are the settings model of a game, its file, and the page that edits it, in the warp_sdk::front::settings module. Settings holds typed values in six groups, and Page draws them on six tabs with one call. The title menu and the pause menu embed the same page, so a game writes the settings screen once. A game reads the fields directly, every frame.

fonts.d: A library of 50 open font families, and a pair picked from a mood
fonts.x: Fonts is a library of 50 open font families and a rule set that picks three faces for a game from a mood and a seed, in the warp_sdk::fonts module. Each game gets a display face for titles, a text face for body text and a mono face for numbers and code. Its reason is that a game that uses the stock font of egui looks like every other game. The same mood and seed always give the same pair, and two moods or two seeds g

cine.d: Film-grammar transitions between screens, easing, and hover animation
cine.x: Cine is a kit of animated transitions between screens and hover animations for buttons, drawn in egui over any game, in the warp_sdk::cine module. A game holds one Cine for its screen enum, asks for a change with one call, and draws each visible screen through a Layer that the kit gives it. The module also holds 22 easing curves and a critically damped Spring. Its premise is that a transition is a sentence in film la

icon.d: An icon drawn in code for the window, the files, and the executable
icon.x: The application icon kit draws an icon in code, so that no Warp application ships without one, in the warp_sdk::icon module. IconSpec::from_name makes a distinct icon from the application name, and a game that wants its own look sets the fields of an IconSpec. One drawing goes to three places: the window, the .png and .ico files, and the .exe file. The renderer runs on the CPU and needs no GPU and no image crate.

boot.d: The native splash a game owns, and PNG screenshots on every platform
boot.x: Boot splash and screenshots are the kit for the first thing that a person sees and for capturing frames, in the warp_sdk::boot module. Splash sets the look of a small native window that shows while the main window waits for its first present. boot::shot saves a frame as a PNG, from the F12 key or from game code. The module re-exports the bootsplash module of warp_core and part of its shot module.

visual.d: One colour, shape and icon set per game role, checked by rule
visual.x: Visual language is the Warp system that gives each kind of thing in a game one role, and each role one colour and one shape, so that a game shows meaning without words. It lives in warp_sdk::visual and its main type is Language. The same role always looks the same, in the world, in the HUD and on the map. The module also holds a vector icon set, colour-blindness simulation, and the bridge to the semiotics icon standa

semiotics.d: One functional standard for game icons, across fonts
semiotics.x: Semiotics is the Warp standard for game iconography, a small visual language in which each action has one meaning class, and each class owns a frame shape, a colour role and a motion. Its code is warp_sdk::semiotics and its text is the document docs/visual-semiotics.md, which requires that a disagreement between the two is fixed in one commit. A one-shot game has almost no text, so its icons carry the rules of the ga

palette-kit.d: Mood-driven palettes, OKLab colour maths and taste rules
palette-kit.x: Palette kit is the Warp module of palettes, colour maths and taste rules, which turns a mood word and a seed into a checked set of colours. It lives in warp_sdk::palette_kit. pick returns a Swatch with one paper colour (bg) and one to five inks, and the seed changes the palette choice, the ink order and a small hue and chroma turn, so two games with two seeds do not get the same look. It is not warp_sdk::palette, the

post.d: One switch per post effect, settable from any thread
post.x: Post effects is the Warp module that controls tonemapping, bloom, colour grade, antialiasing, depth of field, motion blur and the CRT tube through one value with one switch per effect. It lives in warp_sdk::post. Post is a view of the post fields of DisplaySettings, grouped by effect, and a game sets it with one line from new, from gui or from a worker thread. A switch that is off skips the GPU passes of that effect.

camera.d: 2D game camera with follow, dead zone, shake, zoom-to-fit and shots
camera.x: Camera is the Warp 2D game camera, a rig that follows a target with look-ahead and damping, stays inside level bounds, frames groups, shakes from trauma and plays scripted shots. It lives in warp_sdk::camera and its main type is Camera2d. A game makes one camera, calls Camera2d::update once per frame with the frame time and the target position, and sends the result to the renderer. The module header describes it as a

juice.d: Hit-stop, springs, number pops, rings and rumble in one value
juice.x: Juice is the Warp feedback kit, a single value that turns game events into short, time-based effects such as hit-stop, squash and stretch, flash, number pops, rings, button punch, rumble requests and sound requests. It lives in warp_sdk::juice and its hub type is Juice. A game holds one Juice, calls one method per event, advances it once per frame, and paints what it reports. The module header states the purpose as f

lit2d.d: Deferred 2D PBR lighting for material sprites
lit2d.x: Lit2d is the Warp deferred lighting renderer for 2D sprites, which shades each sprite as a surface with albedo, normal, roughness, metallic, height and emissive channels. It lives in warp_sdk::lit2d and its main type is Lit2d. One key light, a hemisphere ambient term and up to MAX_POINT_LIGHTS (256) point lights shade the surfaces, so a flat scene shows the specular highlights and bevel shading of a 3D scene, as Stel

shaderlib.d: WGSL building blocks that a game composes into its own shaders
shaderlib.x: Shader library is the collection of WGSL function files that a Warp game composes into its own shaders. It lives in the module warp_sdk::shaderlib, with one .wgsl file for each block under warp_sdk/shaderlib/, embedded at compile time and validated by cargo test. A game names the files it wants, receives one WGSL string, and appends its own entry points. The library holds functions and structs only. It holds no pipel

shader-noise.d: WGSL hashes, lattice noise, fBm, curl, domain warp and dither
shader-noise.x: Noise shaders are the noise/ category of the shader library, a set of WGSL files that give hashes, lattice and cellular noise, fractal sums, curl fields, domain warp and per-pixel dither. The category is registered in shaderlib::noise. The terrain, post and pattern categories build on it, and every other noise in the library rests on its hash file. All functions start with noise_.

shader-sdf.d: WGSL 2D signed distances, operators, relief, vector fields and polar maps
shader-sdf.x: SDF shaders are the sdf/ category of the shader library, a set of WGSL files for 2D signed distance shapes and for turning a distance into pixels. The category is registered in shaderlib::sdf. It gives primitives, combining operators, coverage and shadow functions, a relief step that lifts a flat shape into a MaterialSample, and two tables of vector fields and polar domains. All functions start with sdf_.

shader-material.d: WGSL procedural surfaces that return a MaterialSample
shader-material.x: Material shaders are the material/ category of the shader library, a set of WGSL functions that compute a lit surface at a world position and return it as a MaterialSample. The category is registered in shaderlib::material. It covers rock, loose ground, metal, wood, ice, flesh and volcanic surfaces, and it adds tools that blend, wet and wear those samples. The main consumer is the lit2d kit, whose material function h

shader-water.d: WGSL caustics, depth fog, plumes, flow, refraction and simulation display
shader-water.x: Water shaders are the water/ category of the shader library, a set of WGSL files for underwater light, water surfaces, flow and the display of simulation textures. The category is registered in shaderlib::water. It covers caustics, Beer-Lambert fog, light shafts, marine snow, vent plumes, glass refraction and colour for fluid fields. All functions start with water_. The GPU simulations themselves belong to the fluid

shader-post.d: WGSL bloom, tonemapping, grading, colour science, sampling, beams and fire
shader-post.x: Post shaders are the post/ category of the shader library, a set of WGSL functions for image processing and light effects. The category is registered in shaderlib::post. It covers a bloom chain, tonemappers, grading, lens effects, film grain, dither, colour spaces, sample sets, beams, volumetric light and fire. All functions start with post_. These are functions and not passes. The engine post-processing chain is a s

shader-organic.d: WGSL corals, plants, fungi and growth patterns as 2D distance fields
shader-organic.x: Organic shaders are the organic/ category of the shader library, a set of WGSL functions that draw corals, plants, fungi and growth patterns as 2D distance fields shaded into a MaterialSample. The category is registered in shaderlib::organic. Forms are parametric and take one species record, so one seed gives one individual. All functions start with organic_. The ports come from Stella Nova reef and plant pages, rewr

shader-creature.d: WGSL layered 2D body plans for fish, jellies, squid, crabs and a submersible
shader-creature.x: Creature shaders are the creature/ category of the shader library, a set of WGSL body plans that draw sea animals and a submersible as layered 2D signed distance fields. The category is registered in shaderlib::creature. Each body plan comes from one parameter record, so a seed gives a stable species, and it returns a MaterialSample. All functions start with creature_. The plans port profile ideas from Stella Nova pa

shader-terrain.d: WGSL caves, DLA ridges, heightfields, strata, reveal and map shading
shader-terrain.x: Terrain shaders are the terrain/ category of the shader library, a set of WGSL functions for side-view caves, top-down heightfields and the shading of ground. The category is registered in shaderlib::terrain. It gives solid and empty fields with signed distance, a per-pixel DLA ridge height, rock strata, line of sight and fog of war, and map colours. All functions start with terrain_. The CPU world kits are separate.

shader-pattern.d: WGSL per-pixel line art, tilings, textiles and seamless pattern motion
shader-pattern.x: Pattern shaders are the pattern/ category of the shader library, a set of WGSL functions that draw graphic patterns per pixel: grids, tilings, mazes, flow lines, textiles, optical art and a Hopf fibration. The category is registered in shaderlib::pattern. Each function returns ink coverage, so a game maps it to its own palette. Two further files stack modifiers on any pattern and loop any pattern seamlessly. All func

squircle.d: the default app UI: corner keys, unfolding panels, toasts, readouts
squircle.x: The squircle kit is the default user interface of a Warp application, drawn over the viewport as corner clusters of squircle keys that unfold into panels. It lives in warp_core/src/ui/squircle and reaches games as warp_sdk::squircle. At rest the screen shows only the viewport and a small cluster of keys. A press on a key unfolds a panel out of it, and a second press retracts the panel into the key. Notices arrive as

hud.d: in-game information: cause cues, world markers, minimap, progress
hud.x: The HUD kit is the family of Warp modules that show a player in-game information with icons and motion in place of prose. It lives in warp_sdk::hud, which holds four submodules that a game reaches by full path, for example warp_sdk::hud::cues . The hud module has no items of its own. Each submodule answers one question a player asks during play.

hud-cues.d: cause and effect shown with icon sentences, pulses, tints and ghost paths
hud-cues.x: HUD cues are short non-verbal signals that show a player why a forced change of state happened. The kit lives in warp_sdk::hud::cues. Its premise is that a forced change with no visible cause reads as a bug: the light goes out, the controls freeze, the camera jumps home, and the player does not know why . A cue answers that with no words.

hud-markers.d: icons pinned to world points, with edge arrows for points off screen
hud-markers.x: HUD markers are icons pinned to world points, with an edge arrow and a distance for any point off screen. The kit lives in warp_sdk::hud::markers. A marker shows where a thing is. When its world point is on screen, the icon sits on the point. When the point is off screen, the icon moves to the screen edge on the line from the screen centre to the point, an arrow points out toward the thing, and a number gives its dis

hud-minimap.d: corner map with fog of war that unfolds to a full-screen map
hud-minimap.x: The HUD minimap is a corner map in a squircle frame that unfolds to a full-screen map on a click or a key. It lives in warp_sdk::hud::minimap. The compact map follows the player from under the key row of a squircle deck. The full map pans with a drag and zooms with the wheel. The map key, Escape, or the close key in its corner retracts it .

hud-progress.d: a stage meter and a short goal list, icon first
hud-progress.x: HUD progress is a pair of displays, a stage meter and a short goal list, that show a player how far they are and what to do now. The kit lives in warp_sdk::hud::progress. Meter shows the first, and Objectives shows the second. Neither uses prose, and a stage name is optional and one or two words .

teach.d: tutorials with control glyphs, verb-keyed steps and purpose cues
teach.x: The teach kit is a set of tools that teach a game by playing it, with pictures in place of a list of words. It lives in warp_sdk::teach. A player learns a game when the game shows them what to do, at the place where they do it, and then shows them that they did it . The kit gives a game three tools for that: Glyph, Course and Cues.

widgets.d: the editor's standard inspector controls, for a game's own tool panel
widgets.x: Panel widgets are the standard inspector controls of the Warp editor, re-exported for a game's own tool panel. The module is warp_sdk::widgets, a re-export of a chosen set from warp_core/src/ui/widgets. Each control takes the full width and reads its colour from the style the engine installs, so a game panel matches the chrome around it . It is for a panel docked in the editor. What a player sees over the game belong

world.d: terrain as a surface field, with collision, biomes, and reveal
world.x: World kit is the family of Warp SDK modules that models a playable place as a surface field, with terrain, collision, biomes, and exploration state. It lives in warp_sdk::world, which holds no code of its own and only declares four submodules. Each submodule has one owner, and games use the full path, for example warp_sdk::world::biome.

world-terrain.d: chunked density field with a dig brush, exact surface, and SDF texture
world-terrain.x: Terrain is a chunked density field that the player can dig, with an exact surface and an exact signed distance near that surface. It is the type Terrain in warp_sdk::world::terrain. A game uses it for a seeded cave or island world, for a Terraria style brush, and as the one source of collision and GPU distance data for the rest of the world kit.

world-collide.d: rays, sweeps, and a circle body against any signed distance field
world-collide.x: Surface collision is the Warp SDK module that moves circles and casts rays against any signed distance field. It lives in warp_sdk::world::collide, and its main field is Terrain. A game uses it to move a body with CircleBody::step, to test sight, and to root props on the ground.

world-biome.d: places that play differently, with blended rules and discovery
world-biome.x: Biomes are places in a Warp game that play differently, not only look different. The module warp_sdk::world::biome defines each place as a Biome, places the set of them in bands with BiomeSet, and gives a blended rule set Env at any point. A biome is a reason to go somewhere.

world-reveal.d: fog of war state with line of sight, save data, minimap, and GPU textures
world-reveal.x: Reveal grid is the Warp SDK structure that records what the player has seen and what the player sees now. It is the type RevealGrid in warp_sdk::world::reveal, and it drives fog of war, a minimap, and cut-away rock. The grid covers a world rectangle with square cells, and each cell keeps two soft values from 0 to 1.

fluid.d: GPU stable fluids and the particles that ride them
fluid.x: Fluid kit is the family of Warp SDK modules that simulates moving water and the particles that ride it on the GPU. It lives in warp_sdk::fluid, which has three submodules and re-exports Ocean and OceanConfig. The one call path for a game is Ocean: the solver, the particles and an optional terrain in one value, with a perf budget.

fluid-solver.d: GPU stable-fluids solver with obstacles, dye, and budgets
fluid-solver.x: Fluid solver is a stable-fluids simulation that runs on wgpu compute shaders. It is the type Solver in warp_sdk::fluid::solver. The solver keeps a velocity field and up to 16 dye channels on a grid that covers one world rect, and it publishes the result as textures. Most games reach it through Ocean, which makes and steps a solver for them.

fluid-particles.d: GPU particles that ride a velocity field and land on terrain
fluid-particles.x: Fluid particles is a GPU particle system for small things that ride a velocity field and land on terrain. It is the type Particles in warp_sdk::fluid::particles, and its presets are marine snow, bubbles, silt and glowing plankton. One compute pass moves all particles, and one instanced draw for each blend mode puts them into the HDR target. The kit works alone, and Ocean also embeds one.

fluid-ocean.d: water, particles, and terrain in one value with a perf budget
fluid-ocean.x: Ocean is the Warp SDK value that combines moving water, the particles that ride it, and the terrain they both hit. It is the type Ocean in warp_sdk::fluid::ocean, re-exported as fluid::Ocean. It is the one call path for a game that wants moving water. An Ocean owns a Solver, a Particles system and, as an option, a Terrain.

procgen.d: seeded streams, Poisson-disc scatter, placement, and fair starts
procgen.x: Procedural generation in Warp is the module warp_sdk::procgen, a set of seeded tools that make a world that is the same on every run. A game makes its world from one u64 seed, and each feature takes its own named stream, so a new feature does not move the old ones. The module also holds Poisson-disc scatter, weighted tables, clusters, surface placement, fair start search, and seed reports. It has no GPU code and depe

challenge.d: combat with damage kinds, statuses, telegraphed attacks and a wave director
challenge.x: Challenge kit is the combat simulation of the Warp SDK: damage kinds, status effects, tools, enemies that warn before they hit, and a director that sets the pace of waves. It lives in the challenge module of warp_sdk. Each enemy resists some damage kinds and is weak to others, so the player must choose a tool and not rely on one general attack. The kit draws nothing: the game reads its state and an event list and dra

economy.d: resources, stores with capacity, costs, recipes, flows and a ledger
economy.x: Economy kit is the resource model of the Warp SDK: resource kinds, stores with capacity, costs, recipes, steady flows, and a ledger of recent changes. It lives in the economy module of warp_sdk. Its purpose is to give the player a reason to collect a thing and a reason to bring it back. A game registers its kinds, makes one Economy, and changes amounts only through it, so each change is recorded for the HUD.

quest.d: objectives and goal chains as plain data, for icons, counts and markers
quest.x: Quest kit is the objective system of the Warp SDK: goal chains held as plain data, with a tracker that counts progress and gives the HUD what to draw. It lives in the quest module of warp_sdk. A game defines a book of Objective values, starts one, and sends the tracker signals as things happen. The tracker keeps a small number of objectives active and reports starts and completions as events.

metaprog.d: unlock trees, stages, upgrades, milestones and a codex that outlast a run
metaprog.x: Metaprogression is the Warp SDK's model of progress that lasts past one moment and past one run: an unlock tree, growth stages, upgrades with levels, milestones and a codex. It lives in the metaprog module of warp_sdk. A game declares its progression as data once, reports what the player does, and reads the events that come back. Meta::save and Meta::load keep the state on disk.

gamepad.d: one verb layer over keyboard, mouse and pad, with input feel helpers
gamepad.x: Gamepad is the input feel layer of the Warp SDK: one set of named verbs over keyboard, mouse and gamepad, with input buffering, coyote time, tap and hold gestures, dead zones, rumble and device-aware button prompts. It lives in the gamepad module of warp_sdk. A game names its verbs once, and each frame it asks about a verb and never about a device. Each part also works alone, with plain f64 seconds.

soundtrack.d: the player's music, tagged ambience and sound effects with ducking
soundtrack.x: Soundtrack is the game-audio layer of the Warp SDK: the player's music, the world's ambience, and sound effects. It lives in the soundtrack module of warp_sdk. Music plays files from a folder that the player picks, Ambience crossfades looped beds by a tag, and Sfx plays one-shot effects with pan, variation and a voice limit. The module's central policy is that the game does not compose music.

net.d: secure host and guest sessions with no server that the developer runs
net.x: Networking in the Warp SDK is the warp_sdk::net module, a set of secure links that let two or more copies of one game share a session with no server that the developer runs. It is a curated view of the warp_net crate, behind the net feature. One peer hosts and holds the canonical state, and the other peers join it as guests. warp_net carries the bytes, keeps them secret, and keeps the link alive. The game decides wha

net-session.d: host, guest and role holder, with seats, channels, blobs, chat and reconnect
net-session.x: Network sessions are the top layer of Warp's networking: the host and guest objects that run the handshake, hold seats, carry application channels and blobs, and survive a dropped link. They live in warp_sdk::net::session, re-exported from the warp_net crate. A session is one host and a set of guests, on any transport that gives a FrameIo. The session layer does not know which transport it runs on.

net-invite.d: one pasted string with the host addresses, port, node id and join code
net-invite.x: Network invites are one-string join tokens: a single text that holds the host addresses, the port, the host P2P node id and the join code, which a guest pastes once. They live in warp_sdk::net::invite, re-exported from warp_net. The codec is pure data in and out. An invite spares the player from typing an address and a code, and a check detects a typo before any connection starts.

net-transports.d: TCP, P2P over QUIC, and a message-sink adapter, each giving a FrameIo
net-transports.x: Network transports are the three carriers under a Warp session: TCP, direct P2P over QUIC, and a message-sink adapter for platform networks. They live in warp_sdk::net::tcp, warp_sdk::net::p2p and warp_sdk::net::msg, re-exported from warp_net. Each one gives a FrameIo, and the session layer runs the same handshake and seal on each. A game picks a transport by what the players can reach.

net-discover.d: UDP beacons that let a guest list the hosts on its local network
net-discover.x: LAN discovery is the Warp SDK's local host listing: a host announces its session by UDP broadcast, and a guest lists the hosts it hears. It lives in warp_sdk::net::discover, re-exported from warp_net. The application holds one Discovery value. A beacon never holds the join code, so discovery only helps a guest find an address.

display-mode.d: window mode, vsync, frame cap and windowed size at run time, from any thread
display-mode.x: Display mode is the run-time state of the primary window: its window mode, vsync, frame cap and windowed size. The display_mode module of warp_sdk reads and changes that state from any thread. A game calls it from new, from gui, from a settings menu or from a worker thread, and the engine applies the change at its next frame.

perf.d: per-system frame budgets, growth detection and automatic quality
perf.x: Perf is the warp_sdk kit that measures frame budgets every frame and adjusts quality automatically. A game gives each costly system a budget in milliseconds, times the system with a guard, and reads one report. The perf module finds three failures: a system over its budget, a system whose time increases over minutes, and a frame too slow for the display. Auto-quality then moves game knobs down until the frame fits, a

gpu.d: formats, post chain, buffers, captures and offscreen targets of the engine
gpu.x: The GPU module is the gpu module of warp_core, re-exported by warp_sdk, which holds the formats, buffers, post-processing chain and readback tools of the engine. A game uses a small part of it: the target formats for its own passes, try_build for optional GPU objects, and the headless hash in gpu::pixhash. Most of the rest is engine plumbing that the module makes public, and several submodules serve editor panels.

render.d: the draw table, registered scene layers and the declared frame graph
render.x: Render passes are the ordered draws that make up a Warp frame, and the render module of warp_core, re-exported by warp_sdk, is the code that owns them. The module holds three things: the table that walks the draw order, the seam through which an application registers scene layers, and a declared frame graph that the engine validates. Layering in the scene is entirely the order of the table.

scene.d: objects with a transform, a parent and a visual, owned by a store
scene.x: The scene is the scene module of warp_core, re-exported by warp_sdk, which holds a general object with a transform, a parent and an appearance, and a registry that owns such objects. An object is drawn because it is in the store, and not because some pass knows how to draw its type. The module uses neither egui nor wgpu, and everything in it runs and is tested with neither.

image.d: mega-atlases, the atlas set descriptor, the disk cache and pak files
image.x: Image atlases are the texture arrays from which Warp draws sprites, and the image module of warp_core, re-exported by warp_sdk, manages them. It holds two atlas kinds, the descriptor through which an application declares them, a disk cache of processed layers, and the packed file format of distribution builds. Which atlases exist and which directories fill them is application data, not engine data.

assets.d: the asset root, path joins and the atlas loader
assets.x: Assets is the module of warp_core, re-exported by warp_sdk, that resolves the asset root directory and joins paths under it. It lets an application run from any working directory or distribution layout. All code that uses an asset calls asset_path and does not build a path by hand. The module holds no asset names: which directories exist is application data that arrives through the atlas set descriptor.

manifest.d: warp_app.toml, the file that states what a project is and how it looks
manifest.x: The app manifest is warp_app.toml, the UTF-8 TOML file through which a hosted application tells the engine its identity, window, assets, atlases and build targets. The manifest module of warp_core, re-exported by warp_sdk, parses and validates the file. The format is the boundary between the engine and one application, so the engine carries no application name of its own. The manifest does not replace Cargo.toml: it

project-settings.d: the registry of [settings.*] blocks that keep a project's look in its manifest
project-settings.x: Project settings is the registry of named settings blocks that live in warp_app.toml under one [settings] table. It is the project_settings module of warp_core, re-exported by warp_sdk. Each subsystem registers a Section, a name with a way to install a table into its global and a way to write that global back. The module owns the file format and the diffing, and a subsystem owns neither.

scale.d: the design-unit scale, the zoom keys and px()
scale.x: Interface scale is the factor by which Warp enlarges every interface measurement and font. The scale module of warp_sdk exposes nine items from the theme code of warp_core, and it is the one part of that theme code that a game receives. The scale is the fix for a problem that every game has, and the palette beside it stays behind.

types.d: shared state and channels that the engine and the application both read
types.x: Types is the types module of warp_core, re-exported by warp_sdk, which holds the shared types and process-global channels that the engine and an application both read. It holds no single concept. The module was one 2700-line file with a dozen unrelated concerns, and it is now a directory with one concern per file, which re-exports all items so that each item keeps its path.

editor-panels.d: every panel a game can feed, and the channels that feed them
editor-panels.x: Editor panels are the tool views of the Warp editor that a running game fills with its own data. Each panel a game drives is one channel, re-exported through warp_sdk. A game publishes to the channels for which it has data, and a game with no editor attached pays almost nothing. The channels share one rule: the game owns the facts, the panel draws them, and anything the panel wants done travels back as data.

census.d: the rows a game publishes for the Hierarchy and Inspector panels
census.x: The census is the channel through which a running application tells the Hierarchy and Inspector panels what exists. The census module of warp_core, re-exported by warp_sdk, carries rows from the application to the panel, and clicks and edits back. A hierarchy panel needs a list of what is alive and a way to say "that one" to its owner, and the engine can supply neither. Each row is a string, an id and a flag word, so

devconsole.d: the Console panel, a mirror of the game's own scrollback
devconsole.x: The dev console is the channel behind the Console panel, a dock panel that shows the console an application already has and types back into it. The devconsole module of warp_core, re-exported by warp_sdk, is the whole of the part that the engine plays. There is one scrollback with two views: a line printed in the game appears in the panel, and a command entered in the panel runs in the game and prints in both.

bindings.d: the table between a key and a verb, read by the input pass and the Control Map
bindings.x: Bindings is the table between a physical input and a game verb. The bindings module of warp_core, re-exported by warp_sdk, lets an application declare its actions once, after which what a key does, what it did by default, what the Control Map panel paints and what a rebind writes are all questions about this one table.

audio.d: the bus a game plays into, and the analysis behind the Audio Scope
audio.x: Audio is the audio module of warp_core, re-exported by warp_sdk, which holds everything the sound monitor reads and the one mixer that a game adopts so that the monitor has a signal. The engine plays no sound of its own. It owns the mixer that the game plays through, so that the mix exists somewhere a tool can reach it. The module is native only, and the bus sits behind the audio feature, which warp_sdk enables by de

palette.d: the fifteen named colours a game draws with, and the box it draws them in
palette.x: Palette roles are a closed vocabulary of fifteen named colours with open values, held by the palette module of warp_core and re-exported by warp_sdk. A game asks for a role and gets a colour. The Theme panel writes the same table, and [settings.theme] in the manifest carries it between runs, so a theme swap is one edit and not a pass over the source.

profile.d: named per-frame spans, the flame chart report, and the Profiler panel
profile.x: The profiler is the profile module of warp_core, re-exported by warp_sdk, which records a stack of named spans per frame and rolls them into the report behind the Profiler panel. The Performance panel says how much a frame cost, but three phases and a population do not form a call tree, and nothing in the engine named the work. These spans are that naming.

hostlink.d: the channel between the editor and the game it launched
hostlink.x: The host link is the channel between the Warp editor and a game that it launched as a separate process. The hostlink module of warp_core, re-exported by warp_sdk, carries a transport that the editor drives, a surface that the game publishes, and each panel channel. It exists because the editor used to link the game, so a project that did not compile took the tool for fixing it down with it. Every call on the game sid

window.d: an application panel in the editor, from two methods
window.x: Custom windows are panels that an application adds to the Warp editor without editing the editor. The window module of warp_core, re-exported by warp_sdk, holds the facts of a window as one struct and one trait, and keeps a process-wide table of them. An author implements WarpWindow, with its two methods spec and ui, calls register before run, and gets a tab, a row in the View menu, a place in the layout, and a tear-

building-a-game.d: Reading order, the kit map, drawing, the one-shot loop, and what to avoid
building-a-game.x: Building a game in Warp is a guide to the order of work for an application on warp_sdk, from the first plan to a passing test suite. It collects what to read, which kit answers which need, how to draw and move things, and which paths to leave alone. The method is a one-shot loop: build a playable path first, prove it with a headless test, and then add systems one at a time.

art-direction.d: Rules for how a Warp game looks, reads and teaches
art-direction.x: Art direction is the Warp guide of rules that make a game look like a product and not like a prototype, covering text, menus, fonts, lighting, density and interface behaviour. It is the document docs/art-direction.md, which a game author reads before the first line of a game. Where building-a-game makes a game run, this guide decides how it looks. Each rule names the SDK kit that implements it, where one exists.
